\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

\looseness=-1 Deploying a pretrained Vision-Language-Action (VLA) model on a new task usually requires fine-tuning on task demonstrations, yet collecting that data is expensive and the resulting checkpoint may not transfer further. A more attractive route keeps the VLA frozen and improves action quality at inference time. Flow-matching VLAs~\cite{black2024pi0,shukor2025smolvla,lipman2023flow} are well suited to this setting because each forward pass produces a stochastic action sample, enabling multi-sample selection and correction without retraining~\cite{snell2024scaling}. But does test-time correction always help? We systematically analyze this question and find that it does not: unconditional correction degrades performance on every suite we evaluate, and the key to making correction useful is knowing \emph{when not} to apply it.

\looseness=-1 Recent work touches parts of this problem without addressing the fundamental question. A2C2~\cite{a2c2_2025} learns a correction head on action chunks but applies it unconditionally and addresses temporal staleness rather than initial action quality. ReconVLA~\cite{chen2026reconvla} quantifies uncertainty over frozen VLAs but does not learn a corrective residual. SC-VLA~\cite{liu2026scvla} uses reinforcement learning and therefore does not stay weight-frozen. VLA-Pilot~\cite{li2025vlapilot} performs evolutionary search at $2.41$\,s per control step, ruling out closed-loop deployment. None analyze when correction helps versus when it hurts, nor provide a mechanism to abstain from correction on confident steps.

\looseness=-1 We begin by analyzing the failure mode of unconditional correction. A lightweight Correction Residual Module (CRM, ${\sim}$327K parameters) trained on demonstration data applies a bounded residual to argmin-selected action samples. Under a K-matched design ($K{=}2$ for both conditions, same $\varepsilon{=}0.2$ and CRM checkpoint), CRM always-on degrades all four LIBERO suites on SmolVLA~\cite{shukor2025smolvla} (0.4B): $-$1.3 to $-$14.8\,pp. The same pattern holds on $\pi_{0.5}$~\cite{black2025pi05} (3.6B, 94--99\% baseline), where unconditional correction degrades all four suites by up to $-$17\,pp. The root cause is that 80--97\% of control steps are already confident; corrections on these steps inject noise rather than signal.

\looseness=-1 This analysis motivates \textbf{ACR-VLA}, an adaptive inference-time pipeline that decides per step whether correction is needed. ACR-VLA draws only $K{=}2$ samples in a single batched forward pass and uses their pairwise $L_2$ distance as a per-step uncertainty probe. This probe is well-calibrated: Spearman $\rho{=}0.9979$ against $K{=}10$ sample variance, whereas three alternatives all yield $\rho < 0.16$. When the probe falls below a threshold $\tau$, the pipeline outputs the argmin-to-centroid sample directly; when it exceeds $\tau$, the CRM applies a bounded residual. The method is a direct consequence of the analysis: once we identify that correction harms confident steps, gating becomes the natural solution.

\looseness=-1 On SmolVLA across four LIBERO suites, ACR-VLA's adaptive gate triggers correction only on high-uncertainty steps (3--20\% of steps), recovering all degradation from unconditional correction: $+$1.5\,pp on Spatial, $+$1.3\,pp on Goal, and baseline-preserving on Object and Long. Under the K-matched design, ACR-VLA exceeds CRM always-on on all four suites ($\Delta_{\mathrm{gate}}{=}{+}2.8$ to $+$14.5\,pp). On $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.6B, 94--99\% baseline), unconditional correction degrades all four suites by up to $-$17\,pp, but adaptive gating recovers 19--50\% of the loss on 3/4 suites, confirming the gate as a safety mechanism even when correction itself provides limited value. A boundary analysis on OpenVLA-OFT~\cite{kim2024openvla} (7B, deterministic) confirms that stochastic sample diversity is a prerequisite.

\looseness=-1 The key finding is mechanistic: \emph{knowing when not to correct} matters more than correction strength. CRM always-on applies the same learned residual to every step, including the ${\sim}$80--97\% where the VLA is already confident; corrections on these steps cause up to $-$14.8\,pp degradation. ACR-VLA's adaptive gate triggers CRM only on high-uncertainty steps, preserving the VLA's own output elsewhere. A threshold sensitivity analysis across three suites (Appendix~\ref{sec:tau_sweep}) shows that success rate is robust to $\tau$ choice, establishing gating as a stable design element rather than a fragile hyperparameter.

Our contributions are:
\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*,nosep]
  \item \textbf{Systematic analysis of test-time correction} (Section~\ref{sec:failure_modes}): under a K-matched design ($K{=}2$, same $\varepsilon$ and CRM), we show that unconditional correction degrades all four LIBERO suites on both SmolVLA ($-$1.3 to $-$14.8\,pp) and $\pi_{0.5}$ ($-$1.2 to $-$17\,pp), identifying the 80--97\% of confident steps as the source of harm.
  \item \textbf{Adaptive gating mechanism} (Section~\ref{sec:method}): a $K{=}2$ pairwise $L_2$ uncertainty probe ($\rho{=}0.9979$) gates CRM correction to the 3--20\% of high-uncertainty steps, recovering all degradation ($\Delta_{\mathrm{gate}}{=}{+}2.8$ to $+$14.5\,pp).
  \item \textbf{Cross-VLA validation} (Section~\ref{sec:cross_vla}): on $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.6B, 94--99\% baseline), adaptive gating recovers 19--50\% of the CRM-induced loss on 3/4 suites; deterministic VLAs (OpenVLA-OFT) produce near-identical samples that make multi-sample methods vacuous.
\end{enumerate}

1	We systematically analyze when test-time correction helps or hurts frozen flow-matching Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models. Applying a learned Correction Residual Module (CRM) unconditionally degrades all four LIBERO suites on SmolVLA (0.4B, up to $-$14.8\,pp on Long) and all four on $\pi_{0.5}$ (3.6B, up to $-$17\,pp)---the 80--97\% of control steps where the VLA is already confident receive corrections that act as noise. This analysis motivates ACR-VLA, an adaptive inference-time pipeline that decides \emph{per step} whether correction is needed. Drawing $K{=}2$ stochastic action samples in a single batched forward pass, ACR-VLA uses their pairwise $L_2$ distance as a per-step uncertainty signal ($\rho{=}0.9979$ against ten-sample variance, zero additional latency) to gate a 327K-parameter CRM. Under a K-matched comparison ($K{=}2$, same $\varepsilon$ and CRM checkpoint), adaptive gating exceeds unconditional correction on all four SmolVLA suites ($\Delta_{\mathrm{gate}}{=}{+}2.8$ to $+$14.5\,pp), with trigger rates of 3--20\% that correlate monotonically with suite difficulty. On $\pi_{0.5}$ (94--99\% baseline), adaptive gating recovers 19--50\% of the CRM-induced loss on 3/4 suites, confirming the gate as a damage-limiting mechanism across capability levels. The key finding is that \emph{knowing when not to correct} matters more than correction strength.
